standing forth with striking clarity, demanding close attention. The entire section on true eminence must be examined in close connection with the overarching theme of this chapter. The line 'straightforward in substance and fond of righteousness' <note>original: "質直好義"</note> expresses his unadorned simplicity and lack of showiness. The two phrases 'observing others' words and examining their expressions' express his inward restraint and absence of unrestrained indulgence. The phrase 'what he does is fitting' in the commentary differs from 'adapting to circumstances according to time' found elsewhere. A scholar of genuine hidden cultivation merely does what ought to be done within his proper station; he never indulges in the bizarre or strange, discarding his fundamental role to perform shocking or sensational deeds. This is precisely where his hidden cultivation takes hold. 'Observing and examining' does not mean spying on the pleasures and angers of others; it refers entirely to his own self-reflection, self-questioning, caution, and reverent awe. The Sage specifically provided this line to lay the foundation for 'taking care to humble oneself beneath others,' with absolutely no emphasis on merely judging oneself. Humbling oneself beneath others denotes inward containment, restraint, and yield, refusing to adopt a grandiose, arrogant demeanor. It is the direct opposite of reckless abandon, not merely the opposite of pride. If one interprets it merely as courteous modesty, the original meaning is lost.

'Plain substance' stands in contrast to superficial decoration; 'straightforward' stands in contrast to deceit and affectation. is so starkly clear and awakening that one must pay close attention. Regarding the section on "attainment" <note>referring to Confucius's description of true inner moral breakthrough in Analects 12.20</note>, one must interpret it by closely adhering to the primary intent of this chapter. The line "straightforward by nature and loving righteousness" describes him as simple, solid, and free of ostentation. The two lines "examining words and observing expressions" describe him as restrained and not self-indulgent. What is noted as "acting in accord with what is right" differs from what is called elsewhere "adapting to the times to establish what is appropriate." A person of genuine hidden cultivation simply does what should be done according to his present station, never acting bizarrely or throwing aside his fundamental duty to perform some extraordinary feat to astonish the world. This is precisely where his hidden cultivation takes hold. "Examining and observing" does not mean prying into other people's joy or anger; it speaks entirely of his own self-reflection, self-questioning, caution, and reverence. The Sage deliberately introduced this line to lay the groundwork for "taking a lower place before others," without emphasizing self-examination alone. "Taking a lower place before others" means restraint, yielding, and avoiding an imposing, self-important posture; it is the opposite of being uninhibited and reckless, not simply the opposite of arrogance.

Yang proceeding to separate yin speaks of the marvelous subtlety of separating and movement from <term>Zhen</term> <gloss>Thunder/Arousing</gloss> growing up to <term>Qian</term> <gloss>Pure Creative</gloss>. This is yang separating yin after the emergence of form. <term>Qian</term> generates a single yin, hence it is said: "The father gives birth to the eldest daughter, which becomes <term>Gou</term> <gloss>Encounter</gloss>." <term>Kun</term> generates a single yang, hence it is said: "The mother conceives the eldest son, which becomes <term>Fu</term> <gloss>Return</gloss>." This combines the yang of Qian and the yin of Kun, taking the entire diagram as a unified discourse.

If one speaks solely of the <term>Wuji</term> <gloss>Ultimateless</gloss>, it resides only in the interval between <term>Kun</term> and <term>Fu</term>, and one cannot point to the realm after the emergence of form to speak of it vaguely. Therefore it is said: "Returning from Kun to Gou is what precedes the Ultimateless." And it is said: "The interval between Kun and Fu is the Ultimateless."

What is meant by "the interval between them"? It is neither movement nor stillness; it is most subtle and most marvelous. This principle exists, yet its traces cannot be seen; it cannot be fully described or depicted.

Master Zhu's poem says: "If you recognize that within nothingness there resides form, I grant that you have personally met with Fu Xi." <note>original: "若識無中含有象，許君親見伏羲來"</note> Truly profound words! Scholars ought to savor them deeply.

The phrase 'straightforward in quality and loving righteousness' <note>Analects 12.20</note> expresses his unadorned simplicity and lack of showiness. The two phrases 'examining words and observing expressions' express his restraint and lack of wantonness. The commentary's gloss 'what he does is appropriate' differs from what is elsewhere called 'making adaptations according to the times'. A scholar of genuine hidden cultivation merely does what should be done according to his proper station. He never engages in bizarre, extraordinary behavior, abandoning his basic duty to perform shocking, world-startling acts. This is precisely the starting point of his hidden cultivation.

'Examining and observing' does not mean spying on the pleasure or anger of others. It entirely speaks to his own self-reckoning, self-questioning, carefulness, and reverent vigilance. The Sage deliberately set down this phrase as a foundation for 'bearing oneself with humility before others' <note>original: "慮以下人" (lu yi xia ren)</note>, and it carries absolutely no sense of scrutinizing oneself in calculation. They represent those scholars of a degenerate age who engage in empty talk about heart-mind and moral nature. The essential tone and meaning of the phrase 'straightforward in quality' means that throughout his life, he is simple and honest, not engaging in cosmetic embellishment. When it comes to his actions, he single-mindedly seeks only what is fitting and proper. To be straightforward in quality is intrinsically the basic capacity of loving righteousness; it is not that outside of this straightforward quality one supplements it with worldly tact. Treat 'quality' as the opposite of cosmetic embellishment. Treat 'straightforward' as the opposite of feigned deceit. A sincere heart has only one straight path, with no winding deviations. # <term>Kan</term> <gloss>The Abysmal Water hexagram</gloss>

<term>Yichuan</term> <gloss>Cheng Yi, Song dynasty Neo-Confucian philosopher</gloss> stated: <term>Xi</term> <gloss>repeated / practiced</gloss> means repeated practice. Although other hexagrams are doubled, the word is not added to their names. <term>Kan</term> alone adds <term>Xi</term> <note>forming Xi Kan, Repeated Pit / Repeated Water</note> because it signifies repeated danger. Within danger there is again danger; its significance is profound. 

In general, when a yang line is at the top, it is the image of stopping <note>Gen, Mountain</note>. When in the middle, it is the image of entrapment and falling into danger <note>Kan, Water</note>. When at the bottom, it is the image of movement <note>Zhen, Thunder</note>. When a yin line is at the top, it is the image of joy and speaking <note>Dui, Lake</note>. When in the middle, it is the image of clinging and brilliance <note>Li, Fire</note>. When at the bottom, it is the image of following and entering <note>Xun, Wind</note>. Entrapment constitutes danger. <term>Xi</term> means repetition, as in learning and reviewing; both carry the meaning of repetition. <term>Kan</term> is danger; what the hexagram discusses is the proper way to conduct oneself in danger and adversity. <term>Kan</term> is water; the number One begins in the middle, being the earliest of generated things; therefore it represents water. Plunging downward is the essential nature of water.

<term>Nanxuan</term> <gloss>Zhang Shi, Song dynasty Neo-Confucian scholar</gloss> stated: <term>Qian</term> <gloss>Heaven</gloss> leads the chant while <term>Kun</term> <gloss>Earth</gloss> harmonizes. <term>Qian</term> is exalted while <term>Kun</term> is humble. This arises from nature and cannot be altered.

<summary>This page introduces the Xi Kan (Repeated Water/Danger) hexagram, opening with Cheng Yi's commentary on why it alone bears the prefix "repeated" to signify stacked perils and the nature of water. Zhang Shi begins to elaborate on the fundamental cosmological harmony and hierarchy between Heaven and Earth.</summary>

Top Six: Wading across the river, submerged over the top of the head. Misfortune, yet no blame. The Image says: The misfortune of wading across the river cannot be blamed.

Master Yichuan <note>Cheng Yi, Song dynasty Neo-Confucian philosopher</note> said: Top Six occupies the ultimate extremity of excess by means of yin-yielding quality. This represents a petty person at the very peak of exceeding ordinary bounds. What is termed "great exceeding" in the case of a petty person does not mean they are capable of performing deeds that surpass others. It simply means exceeding ordinary bounds and transgressing principle, paying no heed to danger or ruin, and walking directly into peril and disaster. It is like crossing water to the point of being completely submerged over the top of the head. The misfortune is obvious. For petty persons to bring disaster upon themselves through rash agitation is only what they deserve. How could any external blame be placed upon it?

<summary>Cheng Yi interprets the Top Six line of Hexagram Da Guo (Great Exceeding), explaining that wading into water over one's head represents petty persons recklessly transgressing principle and inevitably bringing ruin upon themselves.</summary>
<keywords>I Ching, Da Guo, Great Exceeding, Cheng Yi, Yichuan, Top Six, water crossing, hexagram commentary</keywords>

Therefore, the text says "no blame," meaning that since they brought it upon themselves, there is no one else to resent or blame. The meaning of "wading" is drawn from the image of the marsh.

Master Baiyun <note>Kong Wuzhong, Song dynasty scholar</note> said: Earlier scholars took the Top Six line to refer to the affairs of Longfeng <note>Guan Longfeng, loyal minister executed by King Jie of Xia</note> and Bigan <note>Prince Bigan, martyred uncle of King Zhou of Shang</note>, likewise taking "misfortune, yet no blame" as their standard of meaning. However, Longfeng and Bigan were worthy men of firm and upright virtue, not individuals who self-indulgently acted out of yielding weakness. Their path is entirely different from this.

Master Chengzhai <note>Yang Wanli, Song dynasty scholar and poet</note> said: When waters overflow, one who exceeds bounds in wading cannot cross the river, but merely drowns their own crown. One whose responsibility is heavy but whose talent falls short cannot overcome hardship, but only destroys their own person. The commentaries apply this to Wang Yan and Cao Shuang <note>historical officials whose political reach exceeded their capability, resulting in catastrophe</note>.
